passages.title: The official behind the score
passages.text:
A district housing office began using a statistical model to sort applications for subsidised rental homes. The model assigned each application a risk score based on missing documents, reported income changes, previous tenancy disputes and the distance between the applicant's current address and the district office. Applications with higher scores were sent to a caseworker for further examination. The office described the system as a way to direct scarce staff time towards applications that might require more attention.

Within three months, a tenants' group noticed that applicants from two remote settlements were being selected for review far more often than applicants from the town centre. The office initially attributed the difference to a higher frequency of incomplete forms. A later examination showed that residents in the settlements often used seasonal work and changed phone numbers when moving for employment. Their income records therefore appeared less stable, even when their actual earnings were similar to those of other applicants.

The model had not been instructed to disadvantage the settlements. Its developers had trained it on earlier cases in which missing records were associated with higher rates of fraud. But earlier files contained fewer examples from remote communities, and the model treated patterns in that incomplete record as if they described all applicants equally. The score was not a finding of dishonesty, yet officials and applicants began to treat it as one. Some applicants stopped pursuing an application because they assumed a high score meant rejection was inevitable.

The housing office changed its procedure. A high score could now trigger a request for clarification, but it could not determine eligibility or justify refusal by itself. The office published the categories of information used, created a correction route for inaccurate records and required a caseworker to document the reason for any adverse decision. It also began checking outcomes by location and employment pattern, not merely overall accuracy.

The model remained in use, but its role became narrower. It could help organise a queue; it could not replace the official responsible for applying the rules to an individual case. The episode illustrates that an automated system can be technically consistent and still reproduce gaps in the records on which it was trained. Accountability depends on examining both the model and the institution that chooses how to act on its output.

passages.title: Convenience is not consent
passages.text:
A free travel application offered passengers an apparently simple service: it displayed bus arrivals, suggested a route and stored recent journeys so that users could repeat a trip quickly. During installation, the application requested access to location, contacts, photographs and the device microphone. The permission screen grouped all requests under a single button. A passenger who declined could not use even the basic arrival display.

The company said that the additional data would improve route predictions and help identify crowded services. It also used contact data to recommend that friends travel together and microphone access to test a future voice-search feature. Those purposes were not necessary to display a bus timetable. The privacy notice mentioned them in a long list of possible uses, but few users reached the relevant section before accepting the permissions.

A local consumer organisation asked the company to explain why a timetable service needed a passenger's contacts. The company responded that users had voluntarily accepted the permissions and could uninstall the application at any time. That answer treated a single click as if it showed informed agreement to every use of data. It did not explain whether each purpose was optional, how long the information would be retained or whether a passenger could withdraw one permission without losing the basic service.

The company later redesigned the application. Location was requested only while a user asked for nearby arrivals. Contacts and microphone access were moved to separate features and could be declined without blocking the timetable. The application described each purpose before requesting permission, allowed users to delete stored journeys and provided a short explanation of the retention period. The company also separated service analytics from marketing profiles.

The redesign did not remove every privacy trade-off. Location data remained useful for showing nearby buses, and fraud prevention might require some limited technical records. The important change was that users could understand the connection between a data request and the feature they were choosing. Convenience can make a service attractive, but it does not turn unrelated data collection into a necessary condition of access. Consent is meaningful only when the person can see what is being requested and has a practical choice about purposes that are not essential to the service.

A user who wants the basic timetable should not have to surrender access to unrelated parts of a phone. Separate permissions also make the company's own data map clearer: it can identify which feature depends on location and which feature has no need for contacts or audio.

passages.title: The public rail and the private gate
passages.text:
A government built a shared payment network that allowed banks and licensed service providers to send transactions through common technical rules. The network reduced the cost of connecting a new provider and made it easier for a small merchant to accept payments from customers using different applications. The government described the network as public infrastructure, although several private firms developed the applications that customers used every day.

As the network grew, a few applications became the most familiar entry points. Their interfaces offered quick refunds, rewards and customer support. Smaller providers complained that the dominant applications appeared more prominently in search results and that the terms for accessing certain features were difficult to understand. The network operator responded that the payment rail remained interoperable: a customer could transfer money between accounts regardless of which application was used.

Interoperability at the technical layer did not answer every question about access at the service layer. A small provider might technically connect to the network but still struggle to reach users, understand certification requirements or obtain timely support. A consumer might be able to switch applications but lose access to stored transaction history or a reward programme. The infrastructure was open in one sense, while the market for interfaces was becoming concentrated in another.

Regulators began distinguishing the shared rail from the private services built on top of it. They examined whether technical rules were published equally, whether certification decisions had clear reasons and whether a provider could challenge a suspension. They also considered whether consumers had a realistic way to move between applications without losing essential payment functionality. The aim was not to prohibit private innovation but to prevent a public utility from becoming a gate controlled by a small number of interfaces.

The episode shows why the phrase “open infrastructure” needs careful interpretation. A common protocol can reduce barriers at one layer, while commercial practices create barriers at another. Evaluation therefore requires evidence about both the network's technical design and the practical terms under which people and providers use it. Public ownership is not the only route to public value; fair and predictable access can matter just as much.

For a small provider, access may depend on predictable certification timelines and a contact point able to explain a rejection. For a consumer, portability may mean more than moving money: it may also involve retrieving a history, resolving a mistaken debit and obtaining support when a familiar interface disappears.

passages.title: A prediction needs a reason
passages.text:
A public research laboratory developed a model that predicted which rural wells were most likely to fail during the next dry season. The model combined rainfall history, soil conditions, pump age and reports from local engineers. The first version produced a ranked map that helped officials plan inspections. It was praised because several wells identified as high risk later required urgent repair.

When the laboratory shared the map with district officers, they asked for a single score for every village. The score made it easier to allocate inspection teams, but it also concealed uncertainty. Two villages could receive the same score for different reasons: one had a deteriorating pump and reliable rainfall data, while the other had missing records and a model estimate based on neighbouring areas. The same number did not mean that the same evidence supported each prediction.

Engineers also pointed out that some model inputs were out of date. A village had replaced its pump through a local donation, but the central database still listed the old equipment. Another had changed its water source after a road project, a fact recorded in a local meeting but not yet entered into the model. Without a process for correcting those inputs, an official might direct scarce resources away from a village whose risk was understated by stale information.

The laboratory changed its reporting format. Each high-risk result included the factors that contributed to it, the date of the underlying records and a note about missing data. District officers could submit corrections, and an engineer had to confirm material changes before the next ranking. The score remained useful for prioritising inspections, but it was no longer presented as an explanation of why a particular village should receive or lose a service.

The model's value depended on its ability to guide attention without pretending to settle every decision. A prediction can be informative even when it is uncertain, provided that its limitations are visible and people can challenge incorrect inputs. An unexplained number may look precise while concealing the very information needed to judge whether it should be trusted.

The laboratory also began publishing a short model card with each release. It listed the intended use, the groups represented in the test data, known limitations and the date of the last evaluation. The document was not a guarantee of accuracy; it gave users a basis for deciding whether the model was suitable for a particular task.

passages.title: The New Delhi Declaration on AI Impact
passages.text:
The AI Impact Summit 2026 was held in New Delhi on 18 and 19 February. The summit concluded with adoption of the New Delhi Declaration on AI Impact, which was endorsed by 92 countries and international organisations. The declaration presents a shared vision for collaborative, trusted and resilient artificial intelligence and places emphasis on ensuring that the benefits of AI are more widely distributed.

The declaration organises cooperation around seven pillars, described by the summit as “Chakras”. They include development of human capital, broader access for social empowerment, trustworthy AI systems, energy efficiency, use of AI in science, democratising AI resources, and using AI for economic growth and social good. The range matters because AI policy is not confined to model safety or software regulation. Access to computing resources, electricity, skills and public services can determine which countries and communities are able to develop or use the technology.

The declaration is a political statement of shared intent rather than a treaty that automatically creates enforceable obligations for every signatory. Its language supports cooperation and voluntary initiatives while recognising national sovereignty and existing international processes. The endorsement figure therefore indicates the breadth of support for a direction of work, not that all participating governments have adopted identical domestic laws or funding commitments.

The summit also highlighted the need to make AI resources more accessible. Large models require computing infrastructure, data and specialised talent. If those resources remain concentrated in a small number of companies and countries, many organisations may become users of systems they cannot meaningfully inspect, adapt or develop. Broader access can encourage innovation, but it also raises questions about energy use, security, accountability and the ability of smaller institutions to maintain systems over time.

The declaration's practical effect will depend on what governments, research bodies and businesses do after the summit. Useful indicators would include whether training opportunities expand, whether affordable computing becomes available to new users, whether AI systems are tested for reliability and whether public services can demonstrate benefits without excluding people who cannot use digital channels. The declaration creates a framework for cooperation; it does not itself prove that those outcomes have been achieved.

passages.title: The UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance
passages.text:
The inaugural United Nations Global Dialogue on AI Governance was held in Geneva on 6 and 7 July 2026. It was established by General Assembly resolution 79/325, adopted by consensus on 26 August 2025, and was designed as a recurring forum open to all Member States. The Dialogue brought together delegations from 163 countries as well as participants from the private sector, civil society, academia and technical communities.

The Dialogue builds on the Global Digital Compact, which called for international cooperation on digital governance and artificial intelligence. Its format recognises that AI systems are developed and deployed by a mixture of public authorities, private companies, universities and research groups. Governments remain responsible for public policy, but technical expertise and evidence about how systems work may be held outside government. A recurring forum can allow those perspectives to be exchanged without assuming that every participant has the same legal status or decision-making power.

The meeting discussed opportunities and risks associated with AI, including access to infrastructure, safety, human rights, development and the distribution of benefits. It is not a treaty-making body or a supranational regulator. Its purpose is to enable dialogue, identify common ground and inform future work. The co-chairs' summary records discussion and proposals, but it should not be mistaken for a binding rule adopted by every participating country.

The United Nations also presented the preliminary work of the Independent International Scientific Panel on AI during the Geneva meeting. The Panel is intended to provide evidence-based assessments of the opportunities, risks and impacts of AI. Scientific assessment can help policymakers understand areas of agreement and uncertainty, but it does not determine political choices on behalf of Member States. Governments still need to decide how recommendations fit with their legal systems, economic priorities and rights protections.

A second annual Dialogue is scheduled for New York in May 2027. The recurring structure is significant because AI technology and deployment practices change quickly. A single conference may create attention, but sustained governance requires continued evidence, comparison and institutional follow-up. The Dialogue's value will be measured less by the number of speeches delivered than by whether it helps countries understand shared risks and develop practical cooperation while preserving their own responsibilities.

passages.title: India's Digital Personal Data Protection Rules
passages.text:
India notified the Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025, in November 2025 under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023. The Act establishes a framework for the processing of digital personal data and sets out responsibilities for organisations that determine the purpose and means of processing, as well as rights and duties for individuals whose data is processed. The rules provide operational detail for notices, consent and other requirements.

The framework is guided by principles including consent and transparency, purpose limitation, data minimisation, accuracy, storage limitation, security safeguards and accountability. These principles address different stages of data handling. Purpose limitation asks whether information is used for the purpose communicated to the individual. Data minimisation asks whether the organisation collects more information than is needed. Storage limitation concerns how long information is retained, while security safeguards concern protection against unauthorised access, loss or misuse.

The rules were accompanied by a phased commencement schedule. The Gazette notification specified that certain provisions would take effect on publication, others after one year and a further group after eighteen months. This sequencing matters because a notification date does not mean that every operational obligation becomes enforceable on the same day. Organisations need to identify which provisions apply at a given time and prepare for later stages rather than treat the framework as either entirely active or entirely dormant.

The rules also emphasise that consent notices should be clear and specific about the purposes for which personal data is collected and used. A person should be able to understand the request without having to infer every use from a long, undifferentiated list. Clear notices do not eliminate every question about fairness or power. A person may still face practical pressure to accept a request when a service is important or when alternative providers are unavailable.

For organisations, compliance requires more than adding a consent screen. It may involve mapping data flows, limiting collection, correcting inaccurate records, setting retention periods, securing systems and creating procedures to respond to requests. For individuals, rights become meaningful when the routes to exercise them are accessible. The framework's effect will therefore depend on implementation, enforcement, awareness and the quality of systems built around the legal requirements.

passages.title: UNESCO's Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence
passages.text:
UNESCO's Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence was adopted by the organisation's General Conference in November 2021. It is a global normative instrument intended to guide Member States in developing policies and practices for AI. Unlike a treaty, a recommendation does not itself create the same kind of binding legal obligations as an international convention. Its influence depends on how governments and other institutions use it when designing laws, standards and public programmes.

The Recommendation addresses issues across the life cycle of AI systems. It calls attention to human rights, dignity, diversity, fairness, transparency, accountability, sustainability and the need for human oversight. These values are relevant not only when a system is first designed but also when it is tested, deployed, monitored and withdrawn. A system that performs well in a laboratory may produce different effects when used by a public agency or a company serving people with varied languages, incomes and access to technology.

Transparency is not identical to publishing every line of source code. People affected by an AI-assisted decision may need to know that AI was used, what broad factors mattered and how they can challenge an error. Technical details may sometimes be protected for security or intellectual-property reasons, but those limits do not necessarily justify withholding all meaningful information. The level of explanation should be shaped by the impact of the system and the needs of the person affected.

The Recommendation also highlights the importance of assessing impacts before and during deployment. An impact assessment can examine who may benefit, who may be harmed, whether the data are representative and whether safeguards are adequate. Such assessment should not be reduced to a form completed once. New data, model updates and changed operating conditions can create new risks that require renewed attention.

UNESCO's instrument provides a common vocabulary for ethical AI policy and encourages cooperation across countries. It does not certify any particular AI system as ethical, nor does it replace domestic legislation or sector-specific regulation. Its practical value lies in helping institutions ask the right questions about rights, fairness and accountability before technical performance is mistaken for public legitimacy.

passages.title: The International Year of Quantum Science and Technology
passages.text:
The United Nations General Assembly proclaimed 2025 the International Year of Quantum Science and Technology through resolution A/RES/78/287, adopted on 7 June 2024. The observance marked a century of developments associated with modern quantum mechanics and aimed to raise awareness of the importance of quantum science and its applications. It involved scientific institutions, universities, governments and public organisations across different regions.

Quantum science is the foundation for several technologies that are at different stages of maturity. Quantum sensors may enable highly precise measurements; quantum communication research explores methods for protecting information; and quantum computing investigates ways to process certain classes of problems using quantum states. These areas should not be treated as if they have reached the same level of readiness. A laboratory demonstration, a commercially useful device and a broadly deployed service are different milestones.

The International Year also highlighted the need for education and capacity building. Access to advanced laboratories, specialised equipment and trained researchers is uneven across countries. If scientific progress is concentrated in a few institutions, other regions may become dependent on technologies they cannot assess or adapt. International collaboration can expand access to expertise, but it also requires attention to research integrity, security and the distribution of benefits.

Public discussion sometimes treats quantum computing as a machine that will make every conventional computer obsolete. That is not a careful description of the field. Quantum devices may offer advantages for particular tasks, but they are difficult to build and operate, and many practical problems remain. Classical computing will continue to serve most routine applications. A realistic policy response should support fundamental science while avoiding promises that exceed the evidence.

The observance year was a platform for public engagement and international cooperation, not a deadline by which all promised applications had to become commercial products. Its lasting impact will depend on whether education, research networks and institutions continue to develop beyond the calendar year. The resolution called attention to a field of science; it did not itself create a quantum industry or guarantee that each country would gain equal access to its benefits.

The General Assembly's resolution invited scientific organisations, educational institutions and public bodies to use the year to communicate both established findings and open research questions. Public engagement can help students understand why quantum effects matter, but demonstrations should not imply that practical applications are already available at scale. A careful account distinguishes fundamental science from products that remain experimental.

passages.title: NVS-03 and the next phase of NavIC
passages.text:
The Indian Space Research Organisation successfully launched the GSLV-F18/NVS-03 mission on 30 October 2026 from the Satish Dhawan Space Centre at Sriharikota. The GSLV-F18 vehicle placed the NVS-03 navigation satellite into a Geosynchronous Transfer Orbit. A subsequent orbit manoeuvre was completed on 31 October, with further manoeuvres planned to place the satellite in its designated geosynchronous slot. The satellite is the third in a series of five next-generation navigation satellites intended to strengthen the Navigation with Indian Constellation, or NavIC.

NavIC is India's regional satellite navigation system. Satellite navigation services can support transport, timing, emergency response, surveying and other applications that depend on reliable position or time information. A regional system can complement global navigation satellite systems and provide an additional source of service for users within its coverage area. The practical performance of a navigation system depends on satellites, ground control, receiver compatibility, signal quality and the environment in which a device operates.

NVS-03 includes an indigenous atomic clock along with procured atomic clocks. ISRO also described the satellite as including an L1 signal in addition to existing L5 and S-band signals, with coverage over India's landmass and a region extending about 1,500 kilometres around the country's geopolitical boundary. The addition of signal capability can improve compatibility with more receivers, but actual user experience also depends on devices being designed to receive and process the relevant signals.

The launch should be distinguished from the completion of the entire constellation. NVS-03 is one satellite in a planned series, and its placement into a transfer orbit is followed by manoeuvres to reach the intended orbital slot. A successful launch is an important mission milestone, but operational service depends on commissioning, ground-system integration and the availability of compatible user equipment.

The mission illustrates why satellite navigation is both a space capability and a public infrastructure question. A constellation can support strategic autonomy and resilient services, yet its value for citizens and businesses depends on affordable receivers, reliable applications and accurate information about coverage. The launch expands the system's capacity; it does not by itself mean that every device can immediately use every new signal.

passages.title: A score cannot make the final eligibility decision
passages.text:
A public scholarship office uses a software tool to rank applications for manual review. The system compares academic records, household income, attendance and previous scholarship history. Under the office's fictional rule, the score may help identify applications that require clarification, but eligibility must be decided by an officer applying the published criteria. A score alone cannot justify rejection or suspension.

The applicant must be told which category of information has created a concern and be given a practical way to correct an inaccurate record. A notice that says only “risk level: high” is insufficient because the student cannot know whether the concern relates to income, attendance or a missing document. The office need not disclose source code or security-sensitive details, but it must provide the material facts that allow a meaningful response.

A trained officer must review the relevant record and the applicant's explanation before an adverse decision. The officer may accept that a mismatch is harmless, such as an income entry recorded in a different month or an attendance record updated after a medical absence. If the officer rejects the explanation, the written decision must identify the evidence relied upon and explain why the response did not resolve the concern. Repeating the score without independent reasoning is not a review.

The rule allows urgent temporary action where credible independent evidence shows an immediate risk of misuse of funds. Even then, the office must record reasons, set a short review date and provide a prompt appeal route. A software flag by itself is not independent evidence of wrongdoing. If the office discovers that a source database has a systematic error, decisions relying on that field must be paused until a reliable correction process exists.

The rule does not prohibit automated tools. It requires the public institution to remain responsible for decisions made in its name. A model may help organise attention, but eligibility, explanation and appeal remain functions of the office. The affected student must be able to understand and challenge the relevant facts rather than being told that a numerical score has already settled the matter.

Where the applicant is a minor, the notice may also need to be directed to a parent or guardian under the office's procedures. This does not remove the student's interest in understanding the decision. The explanation should be suitable for the people expected to respond and should identify any deadline for submitting a correction or appeal.

passages.title: Consent for a new purpose
passages.text:
A learning application collects a student's name, class level and answers so that it can provide practice questions and record progress. When the application first launches, the student and parent are told that the information will be used to personalise learning and generate reports. Several months later, the provider decides to use the same data to build advertising profiles and share inferred interests with commercial partners. The original notice did not describe that purpose.

For this fictional problem, apply the following rule. Personal information collected for a stated purpose may be used for that purpose and for uses that are reasonably necessary to provide it. A materially different use requires a clear explanation and a valid basis separate from the original permission. The fact that the information is already held does not make every later use permissible. Where consent is the chosen basis, the person must be able to understand the new purpose and make a genuine choice without being misled about the consequences of refusal.

The provider argues that advertising revenue will keep the learning service free. That may be a legitimate business objective, but it does not automatically make advertising profiles necessary to deliver practice questions. The provider could consider less intrusive options, such as contextual advertising that does not rely on an individual's learning history, a paid version or a separate optional feature. It must also consider whether a child or parent can realistically refuse the new use while continuing to access the core educational service.

If the application shares only aggregated statistics that cannot reasonably identify an individual, the analysis may differ. But replacing names with a code does not automatically make information anonymous if the provider or partner can reconnect the record to a student. The provider must examine the practical risk of re-identification and the information available to the recipient.

The rule distinguishes the original service purpose from a new commercial use. It does not prohibit a provider from developing additional features, but it requires the provider to explain the change and obtain the required basis before using existing information in a materially different way. Convenience and business value are not substitutes for a clear purpose and a meaningful choice.

If the provider relies on a statutory basis rather than consent for a particular use, it must still identify that basis and explain the relevant purpose where the rule requires notice. It cannot call a use optional in its public wording while making refusal impossible in practice. The actual design of the service therefore matters as much as the label placed on a button.

passages.title: A known software vulnerability and reasonable care
passages.text:
A company supplies software that stores medical appointment records for a network of clinics. During a routine security review, the company discovers a vulnerability that could allow an unauthorised user to access records if a particular configuration is left unchanged. A software update is available, but installing it requires the clinics to schedule a short maintenance window. The supplier delays informing the clinics because it fears that the announcement will damage confidence in the product.

For this fictional problem, apply the following rule. A service provider that knows of a material security vulnerability must take reasonable steps to reduce the risk and inform affected customers in time for them to protect their systems. The steps required depend on the seriousness of the vulnerability, the likelihood of exploitation, the sensitivity of the information and the availability of a safe remedy. A provider need not disclose technical details in a way that enables attackers to exploit the weakness, but it must give customers enough information to understand the risk and take appropriate action.

The rule also requires reasonable coordination. If an update may interrupt a critical service, the provider should explain the available maintenance options and support customers in applying the fix. It cannot treat operational inconvenience as a reason to leave a known serious vulnerability unaddressed. If exploitation is already suspected, the provider must assist with containment and preserve information needed to investigate the incident.

A clinic may have failed to install an earlier update, but that does not automatically release the supplier from its own duties. Responsibility may depend on the contract, the warnings previously given and the extent to which each party controlled the relevant configuration. The supplier should not assume that a customer's technical team can discover a vulnerability that the supplier has already identified internally.

The rule does not demand perfect security. It requires reasonable prevention, timely communication and cooperation in response to known risks. A provider that hides a serious weakness to protect reputation may increase harm to customers and patients. Security is an ongoing process, and the duty to act depends on what the provider knows and what practical steps are available.

The provider should also distinguish between a vulnerability that is merely theoretical and one that can be exploited under the customer's actual configuration. A risk notice can describe the affected versions, recommended mitigation and expected service interruption without publishing a step-by-step exploit. The rule requires enough information for protection, not instructions that create a new danger.

passages.title: A synthetic recording presented as genuine
passages.text:
A local election committee receives an audio recording in which a candidate appears to instruct supporters to damage a rival's campaign office. The recording is widely shared. A technical consultant says that the file contains signs of synthetic generation, while the person who supplied it insists that it is an authentic voice message. The committee must decide whether to rely on it when considering a complaint under its fictional conduct rules.

For this fictional problem, apply the following rule. A recording may be considered as evidence only after the decision-maker examines its provenance, integrity and context. A file's apparent voice similarity is not enough to establish that the named person created or approved it. Relevant checks may include the original source, the chain of custody, signs of editing, metadata, corroborating evidence and whether the recording is complete. A technical assessment may assist, but its limitations must be disclosed.

The committee must give the person accused a fair opportunity to respond to the material relied upon. It may protect the identity of a witness where necessary, but should provide enough information about the allegation for a meaningful response. If the recording cannot be authenticated, the committee may consider other independent evidence; it cannot treat uncertainty as proof of guilt. Equally, a claim that a recording is synthetic does not automatically prove that it is false.

The rule does not require the committee to establish every technical detail beyond all doubt. It requires a reasoned assessment of reliability and a decision based on the total available evidence. If the consultant can identify likely manipulation but cannot determine who created it, the committee should state that limitation rather than attribute responsibility to a particular person without support.

The distinction between a file and the event it purports to record is central. Digital evidence can be persuasive because it appears precise and immediate, but its authenticity and context still require examination. The decision-maker remains responsible for explaining why the material is accepted, rejected or treated as inconclusive.

If the recording is circulated before the committee completes its review, the committee should avoid repeating the allegation as an established fact. It may issue a neutral notice that the material is being examined and remind participants not to harass either the candidate or the person who supplied the file. A precautionary response does not determine the final evidentiary question.

passages.title: A decision needs reasons that can be used
passages.text:
A public transport authority uses a model to decide which applicants qualify for discounted travel passes. A passenger receives a message stating that the application has been rejected because the applicant's “eligibility index” fell below the required threshold. The passenger cannot see which information produced the index and has no way to correct a mistaken address or income record.

For this fictional problem, apply the following rule. Where a public authority makes an adverse decision that materially affects access to a public service, it must provide reasons sufficient for the affected person to understand the main basis of the decision and identify any relevant factual error. The authority need not publish its entire source code or disclose security-sensitive information. It must, however, explain the material categories considered and provide a route to challenge inaccurate or incomplete information.

The authority argues that a detailed explanation would make it easier for applicants to manipulate the system. The rule permits it to withhold narrow operational details where disclosure creates a demonstrated risk, but that concern cannot justify a message that gives no usable explanation at all. It may describe the relevant category, such as household income or residence, without revealing the precise detection threshold. An independent reviewer can examine whether the withheld detail is genuinely sensitive.

If the passenger shows that the address in the application was mistyped, the authority should correct the record and reconsider the decision. It need not grant the pass automatically if other eligibility conditions remain unsatisfied. The purpose of review is to ensure that the decision is based on accurate information and the published criteria, not to guarantee a favourable result.

The rule distinguishes an explanation that is technically detailed from one that is practically useful. A long report may reveal little if it does not identify the fact that affected the applicant. A concise notice can be adequate when it shows the relevant basis and tells the person how to correct it. The authority must remain able to explain the decision in terms that connect its model to the rules it is responsible for applying.

Reasons are also relevant to internal review. A second officer should be able to see which published criterion was applied and whether the underlying record was accurate. If the first officer cannot explain the result beyond repeating a score, the review process cannot test whether the model's output was used properly.

passages.title: Changing the rules of a digital platform
passages.text:
A digital marketplace publishes rules stating how sellers may list products, how complaints are investigated and when an account may be suspended. Small sellers rely on the platform to reach customers and plan stock purchases around the published fee schedule. The platform later changes its algorithm and begins charging a new visibility fee. It applies the change immediately to existing listings without notifying sellers or explaining how the fee affects product ranking.

For this fictional problem, apply the following rule. A platform may revise its operating terms for legitimate business reasons, but a material change affecting existing users must be communicated clearly and with reasonable notice before it takes effect, unless an urgent security or legal reason requires immediate action. The platform must describe the practical effect of the change and provide a route for users to ask questions or close their account without being misled. A term that allows unlimited unilateral changes does not remove the obligation to act fairly.

The platform argues that sellers can leave whenever they wish. That option may be relevant, but it does not necessarily cure a sudden change after sellers have bought inventory or committed to advertising. A reasonable transition period allows users to adapt, cancel planned listings or compare alternatives. The required notice may depend on the magnitude of the change and the degree of reliance the platform could reasonably foresee.

If a security incident requires the platform to suspend a compromised account immediately, it may do so without the ordinary notice period. It should still provide a prompt explanation once disclosure is safe and allow the seller to challenge a mistaken identification. An urgent protective measure should not become a pretext for imposing an unrelated commercial term without notice.

The rule recognises that digital services need flexibility, but also that users organise real economic activity around platform rules. Fairness depends on the materiality of the change, the notice given, the ability to adapt and the reasons for any immediate action. The platform remains responsible for explaining how its published system has changed.

The platform should retain the earlier terms and the date on which each version applied. If a seller complains that a new fee was applied before notice, the record can show what the seller was told and when. Version control does not decide whether a change is fair, but it makes the decision easier to examine.

passages.title: Benchmark performance and deployment risk
passages.text:
A technology agency reports that a new language model achieved a higher score than its predecessor on a set of standardised reasoning tests. The agency concludes that the new model is safer for use in public services because it makes fewer errors on the benchmark. The report is based on thousands of test questions and has been reviewed by an external laboratory.

The improvement is meaningful within the limits of the test. However, the benchmark contains short, clearly stated questions and does not reproduce the conditions under which people approach a public service. A user may provide incomplete information, use a regional language, describe a problem indirectly or ask for help while under stress. The system may also be connected to databases or tools that introduce errors not present in the benchmark.

A second issue concerns the nature of the errors. A model may improve its average score by answering more common questions correctly while continuing to fail on a small group of high-consequence cases. If the agency uses the model to explain benefit eligibility, a wrong answer about an appeal deadline may matter more than several correct answers about general information. A single average score hides the distribution and seriousness of mistakes.

The agency proposes a staged trial. It will test the model on realistic enquiries, compare performance across languages and user groups, measure the frequency of harmful errors and keep a human officer responsible for final decisions. It will also record cases where users abandon the interaction or seek help elsewhere. The benchmark score remains one part of the evidence, not the final test of suitability.

The report's conclusion is therefore stronger than its data justify. Better benchmark performance is evidence of progress on the tasks measured. It does not automatically establish safety in every deployment. A responsible evaluation asks whether the test resembles actual use, whether errors are distributed fairly and whether the institution can detect and correct failures after release.

The agency could also test whether the model's advantage persists when questions are asked in languages and formats that were underrepresented in its benchmark. A deployment evaluation should include users who need assistive technology and people who provide partial information. If the model performs well only for a narrow test population, the headline improvement may not transfer to the public service.

passages.title: Offline alternatives and resilience
passages.text:
A city replaces paper appointment slips at public clinics with a mobile application. Within six months, online bookings rise and the average time spent at the registration counter falls. The health department concludes that the digital system has made access more efficient and proposes closing the remaining walk-in desk at smaller clinics.

The figures describe users who successfully booked online. They do not reveal how many people tried and failed, how many lacked a compatible phone or how often the network was unavailable. In neighbourhoods with reliable connectivity, the application may reduce waiting. In remote areas, a resident may travel to a clinic only to learn that the booking system cannot verify an identity record. A lower counter queue does not necessarily mean that fewer people were unable to obtain an appointment.

The department argues that maintaining a walk-in desk is expensive and that most residents now own a smartphone. Ownership alone does not prove that a person can complete a form, receive a one-time password or understand an error message. A phone may be shared by several family members, or the data connection may be unavailable at the time the appointment is needed. A system that assumes continuous access may work well in ordinary conditions and fail precisely when demand is high.

A more complete evaluation would measure successful appointment completion across channels, not only online submissions. It would also record failed attempts, abandoned journeys and the use of assisted booking. The department could maintain a smaller assisted desk or an offline queue that syncs records when connectivity returns. That arrangement would retain most of the digital efficiency while providing a fallback for people excluded by the technology.

The question is not whether digital services are preferable to paper in every case. It is whether the system remains usable when devices, connectivity or identity records fail. Resilience includes the capacity to continue serving people during disruption. A channel that disappears when its supporting infrastructure fails should not be treated as the only measure of successful modernisation.

The department should also compare the cost of assisted access with the cost of failed appointments. An offline route may appear less efficient when measured as staff time per booking, but it can prevent a person from making repeated journeys after a digital failure. The proper comparison includes successful access, not simply the cost of processing a completed online form.

passages.title: More data can reduce trust
passages.text:
A municipal safety unit installs additional cameras and proposes linking their footage with travel-card records to identify crowding and respond to emergencies. Officials argue that more information will allow faster decisions and reduce the risk of missing a dangerous incident. The system is expected to help planners understand how people move through crowded spaces.

A civil-society group agrees that accurate information can improve safety but questions whether every data source is necessary. The unit has not shown that linking individual travel histories is required to estimate crowd density. It could use aggregated counts or short retention periods for much of the planning work. Linking identifiable records may create a detailed history of a person's movements that could later be used for unrelated purposes.

The unit replies that safeguards can be added after launch. Yet trust depends partly on what people understand before data collection begins. If residents believe that every journey is being recorded without a clear purpose, they may avoid public transport or change their behaviour. That response can make the data less representative and undermine the very planning objective the unit wants to support.

A pilot could compare several methods. One would use camera-based counts that do not identify individuals; another would link records only for a limited emergency investigation under a defined authorisation process. The unit could measure response time, false alerts, retention needs and public understanding. It should explain what information is collected, who can access it and when it is deleted. The choice should be based on evidence of necessity and effectiveness rather than the assumption that more data always produces better decisions.

The safety objective is legitimate, but it does not settle the scope of collection. More information may improve a system when it is relevant and reliable. Unnecessary collection can increase risk, cost and public resistance. A successful design must consider both operational performance and the conditions that make people willing to use a public service.

The unit could also publish a retention schedule and an audit record of who accessed identifiable footage. Independent review may help determine whether the safety benefit justifies the collection and whether less intrusive information would have achieved the same result. These safeguards will not remove every concern, but they allow the public to examine whether the stated purpose is being respected.

passages.title: An explanation must permit correction
passages.text:
A university deploys an automated system to identify students who may need additional academic support. It sends a notice when a student's activity falls below a threshold and recommends a meeting with an adviser. The university describes the system as supportive rather than punitive, and says students can contact the office if they disagree with the result.

Students soon discover that the notice does not identify which activity triggered it. One student had completed assignments offline during a platform outage; another had changed courses and was no longer required to use the earlier online module. Both received the same notice. The university's staff could see the score but not a clear explanation of the inputs that determined it.

The university argues that showing a detailed explanation may reveal how to avoid detection. But the purpose is to offer support, not to catch misconduct. A student who does not know whether the notice concerns attendance, course registration or assignment submission cannot correct the relevant record. The general invitation to contact the office places the burden on the student to guess what went wrong.

A revised process shows the categories contributing to the alert and the date of the records used. Students can correct a course enrolment or report a platform outage. Advisers review the corrected information before recommending support. The university still protects technical details that would compromise system security, but it no longer treats a score as a sufficient explanation.

The change does not require every automated system to reveal every internal calculation. It requires a level of explanation that matches the purpose and impact of the system. Where the institution expects people to act on a notice, it must give them enough information to understand what is being asked and to correct a material error. Without that possibility, the promise of supportive intervention may become an unexplained label attached to the student.

The institution should also tell the student how long a correction request is expected to take and what happens while it is being considered. A route that exists only on paper may not help someone who needs support immediately. Practical contestability therefore includes a reachable contact, a reasonable response time and a way to avoid an adverse label while a material record error is being checked.

passages.title: Shared AI compute allocation
passages.text: A public research centre has 1,200 accelerator-hours available in one week. University A receives 35%, University B receives 25% and start-up teams share the remainder. Of the start-up allocation, 40% is reserved for safety testing and the rest for general research. During the week, University A uses 90% of its allocation and University B uses 80%. The centre charges ₹500 per used accelerator-hour for external users. Treat all percentages as exact and ignore taxes.

passages.title: Digital wallet transaction study
passages.text:
A payment network processes 80,000 transactions in a month. Forty-five per cent are small-merchant payments, 30% are bill payments and the remainder are person-to-person transfers. Of small-merchant payments, 4% are reversed; of bill payments, 2% are reversed; and 1% of person-to-person transfers are reversed. A separate audit finds 600 transactions requiring manual review. Assume the three transaction categories are mutually exclusive and exhaustive.

The network's finance team reports reversals separately from the manual-review count. A transaction may be reversed without requiring manual review, and a transaction flagged for review may ultimately be valid. Do not assume that the two groups are identical or add them together unless a question explicitly asks for their combined total.

passages.title: Cyber incident response
passages.text: A service provider receives 2,400 security alerts in a quarter. Thirty per cent are classified as high priority, 45% as medium priority and the remainder as low priority. Analysts resolve 80% of high-priority alerts, 75% of medium-priority alerts and 90% of low-priority alerts within the target time. Each resolved high-priority alert requires an average of 3 analyst-hours, each medium alert 1.5 hours and each low alert 0.5 hour. Assume the stated percentages are exact.
